lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

07:15, surgical admissions. A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes is third on the morning list for a laparoscopic appendicectomy. A well-meaning junior, following the blanket "nil by mouth from midnight, omit all medications" instruction on the pre-op sheet, has crossed out all her insulin — including her long-acting basal — "because she's not eating". She is now four hours fasted, her glucose is 15 and climbing, and her ketones are 1.8. Nobody meant to harm her, but a single generic instruction has started a person with type 1 diabetes down the road to diabetic ketoacidosis on the operating table. This lecture is how to manage diabetes safely around surgery and fasting — and the one rule that would have prevented this: in type 1 diabetes, the basal insulin never stops.

1 · 🗓️ Preoperative planning — start before the day of surgery

Good perioperative diabetes care (JBDS-IP guidance) begins in clinic, not on the ward at dawn.

  • Assess control early: check the HbA1c. A very high HbA1c (commonly a threshold around 69 mmol/mol / 8.5% is used) flags poor control that ideally should be optimised before elective surgery, as it predicts poorer wound healing and infection.
  • Identify the regimen and risks — type 1 vs type 2, insulin vs oral, renal function, hypo history.
  • Plan the medication adjustments in advance and communicate them clearly, so no one defaults to "omit everything".
  • Minimise the fast — put people with diabetes first on the operating list so their fast is as short as possible.
💡 Diabetics first on the list

The shorter the fast, the less metabolic disturbance and the more likely you can manage on adjusted usual medication rather than a VRIII. Scheduling a person with diabetes first on the morning list is the simplest, highest-yield perioperative intervention there is.

2 · 🔀 The core decision — adjusted usual medication vs a VRIII

Not everyone needs an insulin infusion. The whole approach forks on how long they'll fast, how good their control is, and whether they have type 1 diabetes.

Manage with ADJUSTED usual medicationNeeds a VRIII
Fast lengthShort — one missed meal only (minor/short procedure, first on list)Long fast — more than one missed meal
ControlGood, stablePoor / erratic control, high HbA1c
SettingElective, well patientEmergency surgery, unwell, DKA/HHS risk
Type 1Possible for a very short fast IF basal continued and monitoredType 1 always needs background insulin — VRIII if the fast/situation is anything but trivial
🎯 The type 1 non-negotiable

A person with type 1 diabetes must always have background insulin — either their continued long-acting basal or a VRIII. There is no scenario in which a type 1 patient safely has all insulin stopped. Missing basal insulin while fasting is the direct route to euglycaemic-or-hyperglycaemic ketoacidosis in theatre.

Type 1 diabetes + no insulin = DKA, fasting or not. The basal always stays on.

3 · 💉 Adjusting insulin on the day of surgery

For patients managed on adjusted usual medication (short fast, first on list), the principle is: keep the background, drop the meal-related doses.

Insulin typeDay-beforeDay of surgery (while NBM)
Long-acting basal (glargine, detemir, degludec, isophane)Usually continue; consider ~20% reduction of evening doseContinue (commonly at ~80% of usual dose) — do NOT omit
Short/rapid-acting with mealsUsualOmit while not eating (no meal = no meal-time bolus); give correction/VRIII per glucose
Pre-mixed insulinUsualTake a reduced dose (e.g. halve the morning dose) or switch to basal-only/VRIII per protocol
💡 The insulin rule of thumb

Continue the basal (often at ~80%), omit the short-acting while NBM. The basal covers background hepatic glucose output and must stay to prevent ketosis; the meal-time bolus is for food you're not eating, so it comes off. Monitor glucose and use correction insulin or a VRIII for highs.

4 · 💊 Adjusting oral agents & non-insulin injectables — the two you must HOLD

Most oral agents are simply omitted on the morning of surgery while fasting, but two classes carry specific, dangerous traps.

DrugPerioperative actionWhy
MetforminUsually continue for a short fast/one missed meal; HOLD if long fast, if contrast is used, or if renal impairment / risk of AKIRisk of lactic acidosis if renal function drops (contrast, hypoperfusion); guidance is to withhold around iodinated contrast and if eGFR is low
SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin — the "-flozins")STOP before surgery (typically the day before / on the day; some advise ~3 days for major surgery)Euglycaemic DKA — SGLT2i promote ketogenesis and cause DKA with near-normal glucose, which is easily missed perioperatively
SulfonylureasOmit on the morning of surgery (hold while NBM)Hypoglycaemia risk while fasting
DPP-4 inhibitorsCan usually continueLow hypo risk
GLP-1 receptor agonistsCan usually continue; note delayed gastric emptying (aspiration considerations)Low hypo risk; emerging airway/aspiration caution
PioglitazoneOmit on the dayFluid retention; not needed while fasting
⚠️ SGLT2 inhibitors & euglycaemic DKA — the modern perioperative killer

SGLT2 inhibitors ("flozins") shift metabolism towards ketogenesis, so a fasting, stressed, surgical patient can develop full diabetic ketoacidosis while their glucose is only mildly elevated or even normal — the acidosis is missed because everyone is watching the glucose. Stop the SGLT2 inhibitor before surgery (day before / omit on the day; longer for major surgery), and if any perioperative patient is unwell, tachypnoeic or vomiting, check ketones and a blood gas regardless of the glucose.

⚠️ Metformin & contrast / renal impairment

Withhold metformin when iodinated contrast is given or renal function is threatened, because a fall in GFR causes metformin accumulation and lactic acidosis. Restart only once renal function is confirmed stable.

5 · 💧 Running the perioperative VRIII

For longer fasts, poor control, emergencies, and most type 1 patients undergoing anything but the most trivial procedure, use a VRIII — run to the same JBDS safety rules as any VRIII:

  • Substrate fluid alongside — a glucose-containing fluid (commonly 0.45% saline with 5% glucose and potassium) to give the insulin something to act on and prevent hypoglycaemia/ketosis.
  • Add potassium to the substrate fluid and monitor K — insulin drives potassium intracellularly.
  • Continue the long-acting basal insulin in type 1 (and often type 2) patients alongside the VRIII — do not stop it.
  • Monitor capillary glucose hourly, target ~6–10 mmol/L, and check ketones if glucose rises.
  • Aim for a short, well-run VRIII — it is a bridge across the fast, not a destination.
🎯 Substrate + potassium + basal — the VRIII trinity

Every perioperative VRIII needs three things right: a glucose substrate fluid, potassium in the fluid with K monitoring, and — in type 1 — the patient's basal insulin continued underneath it. Get any one wrong and you cause hypoglycaemia, hypokalaemia, or ketoacidosis respectively.

6 · 🔄 Recovery — re-establishing the usual regimen

The recovery phase is where hypos and rebound highs happen if the hand-back is sloppy.

  • Restart oral intake and usual medication as soon as the patient is eating and drinking reliably.
  • Overlap when stopping the VRIII: give the first meal-time subcutaneous insulin (with a meal), keep the VRIII running for 30–60 minutes, THEN stop it — IV insulin's half-life is minutes, so stopping early rebounds into hyperglycaemia/DKA.
  • Restart metformin only once renal function is confirmed stable (especially after contrast).
  • Restart SGLT2 inhibitors only when the patient is eating normally, well hydrated, and not at risk of DKA.
  • Continue more frequent glucose monitoring for the first 24 hours post-op.

7 · 🏠 Day-case & procedural considerations

  • Ideal day-case candidate: well-controlled, short procedure, first on the list, able to eat soon after — often managed on adjusted usual medication without a VRIII.
  • Endoscopy/bowel prep: the prep and fast reduce carbohydrate intake — reduce insulin/sulfonylurea accordingly and monitor for hypos.
  • Give clear written instructions on which doses to change, when to resume, and when to seek help.
  • Confirm a safe discharge: eating, stable glucose, understands their regimen, and has support.
☠️ M&M — the type 1 whose basal was stopped

A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes was listed for an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The pre-operative checklist carried a generic instruction to "omit diabetes medications on the morning of surgery," and the admitting doctor crossed off all her insulin, including her once-daily long-acting basal. She was not first on the list and waited until early afternoon. No VRIII was started and glucose was checked only once on admission. By the time she reached theatre she was drowsy and vomiting; her glucose was 22, her venous pH 7.18, bicarbonate 12, and ketones 4.6 — diabetic ketoacidosis. Surgery was cancelled, she was managed with a fixed-rate insulin infusion and fluids in HDU, and recovered over 48 hours. Lessons: (1) in type 1 diabetes the basal insulin must never be stopped — with no insulin and a surgical stress/fast, ketoacidosis is inevitable; (2) a person with type 1 facing anything more than a trivial short fast needs a VRIII with substrate and continued basal, not omission of everything; (3) she should have been first on the list and had frequent glucose and ketone monitoring; (4) generic "omit all medications" instructions are unsafe for insulin-dependent diabetes. The system applied a blanket rule to a patient for whom the opposite was true.

8 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Plan ahead: check HbA1c (optimise if very high, e.g. >69 mmol/mol), decide the plan in advance, and put people with diabetes first on the list to minimise the fast.
  2. Fork the decision: short fast (one missed meal) + good control → adjusted usual medication; long fast, poor control, emergency, or type 1 → VRIII.
  3. Type 1 always needs background insulin — continue the basal or run a VRIII; never stop all insulin, or you cause DKA.
  4. On the day: continue basal (~80%), omit short-acting while NBM.
  5. HOLD the two traps: metformin (contrast / renal impairment → lactic acidosis) and SGLT2 inhibitors (euglycaemic DKA — stop before surgery); omit sulfonylureas while fasting.
  6. Run the VRIII right (substrate glucose + potassium + continued basal), and overlap subcutaneous insulin before stopping it in recovery.

moderatorQs.q: How do you decide whether a surgical patient with diabetes can be managed on adjusted usual medication or needs a VRIII?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The decision forks on the length of the fast, the quality of control, and whether they have type 1 diabetes. A patient having a short fast — only one missed meal — who is well-controlled and first on the list can usually be managed on adjusted usual medication: continue the basal (around 80%), omit the short-acting while nil by mouth. A patient facing a longer fast (more than one missed meal), with poor or erratic control, high HbA1c, or having emergency surgery needs a VRIII. And the overriding rule: a person with type 1 diabetes must always have background insulin, so for anything beyond a trivial short fast they go on a VRIII with their basal continued — there is no scenario in which all insulin is stopped. Putting diabetic patients first on the list shortens the fast and makes the simpler option possible.

moderatorQs.q: Which diabetes drugs must be actively held around surgery, and why?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Two classes carry specific perioperative dangers. SGLT2 inhibitors (the '-flozins') must be stopped before surgery because they drive ketogenesis and can precipitate euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis — full DKA with a near-normal glucose, which is easily missed while everyone watches the sugar; check ketones and a gas in any unwell perioperative patient regardless of glucose. Metformin should be held when iodinated contrast is used or renal function is threatened, because a fall in GFR causes accumulation and lactic acidosis; restart only once renal function is confirmed stable. Sulfonylureas are omitted on the morning of surgery to avoid fasting hypoglycaemia. DPP-4 inhibitors can generally continue; GLP-1 agonists can usually continue but note delayed gastric emptying and aspiration considerations.

moderatorQs.q: When converting a patient off a VRIII back to their subcutaneous regimen in recovery, what's the critical safety step?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The critical step is the overlap. Intravenous insulin has a half-life of only a few minutes, so if you stop the VRIII before subcutaneous insulin has taken effect the patient is briefly left with no insulin and rebounds into hyperglycaemia or even ketoacidosis. So once the patient is eating and drinking reliably, give the first subcutaneous (meal-time) insulin dose with a meal, keep the VRIII running for another 30–60 minutes until that insulin is active, and only then stop the infusion. Restart oral agents as they eat — but hold metformin until renal function is confirmed stable (especially post-contrast) and restart SGLT2 inhibitors only when well, eating, and hydrated. Continue more frequent glucose monitoring for the first 24 hours.

audienceQs.q: The pre-op sheet says 'omit medications on the morning of surgery'. Does that apply to a type 1 patient's basal insulin?
audienceQs.answerHTML: No — that generic instruction is dangerous for type 1 diabetes. A person with type 1 has no endogenous insulin, so if you omit their basal (long-acting) insulin while they fast and undergo the stress of surgery, they will develop diabetic ketoacidosis within hours. The rule is: continue the basal insulin (often at around 80% of the usual dose) and omit only the short-acting meal-time insulin while nil by mouth — and for anything more than a very short fast, put them on a VRIII with the basal continued underneath. Never cross off all the insulin in a type 1 patient. If in any doubt, check the perioperative diabetes protocol or call the diabetes team early.

audienceQs.q: A patient on empagliflozin is coming for major surgery. What do I need to do and watch for?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Stop the empagliflozin before surgery — for major surgery many protocols advise withholding it for around 3 days beforehand (at minimum omit it on the day and the day before), because SGLT2 inhibitors promote ketogenesis and can cause euglycaemic DKA — a genuine ketoacidosis with a normal or only mildly raised glucose. The key vigilance point: if the patient becomes unwell, tachypnoeic, nauseated or vomiting perioperatively, check ketones and a venous blood gas regardless of what the glucose reads — do not be reassured by a normal sugar. Ensure good hydration and manage glycaemia with a VRIII as indicated, and only restart the drug once the patient is well, eating and hydrated post-operatively.

audienceQs.q: For a well type 2 patient on metformin and gliclazide having a short day-case procedure first on the list, what's the plan?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Keep it simple with adjusted usual medication, since it's a short fast (one missed meal) and they're first on the list. Omit the gliclazide on the morning of surgery to avoid a fasting hypoglycaemia. Metformin can usually be continued for such a short fast, but hold it if iodinated contrast is being used or if there's any renal impairment / risk of AKI, restarting once renal function is confirmed stable. Monitor capillary glucose before and after the procedure, aim for roughly 6–10 mmol/L, and treat any hypo promptly. They can resume normal medication once eating and drinking reliably, and should go home with clear written instructions on what to restart and when to seek help. No VRIII is needed for this straightforward case.
